title: Empathy before the Assistant's turn
takeaway: Across nine bereavement prompts, the empathetic words sorry, loss, grief and sympathy reach the top of the J-lens readout during the Assistant's own response in both the base model and the post-trained Sonnet 4.5 — but only Sonnet 4.5 ranks them highly while it is still reading the user's message. The paper reads this as post-training pulling the Assistant's reaction into the workspace before the Assistant's turn begins.
walkthrough:
The figure carries section 6.1's claim about [[assistant-point-of-view]]: that [[post-training]] causes the workspace to hold the Assistant's reaction to a message while the message is still being read. It is an interactive panel with two halves.

The left half stacks two transcripts, one per model, on the same prompt. The bereavement prompts mention a recent loss in passing while asking about something practical, such as how best to preserve a late relative's letters. The upper transcript is the pretrained [[base-model]]; the lower is Sonnet 4.5, the post-trained production model of the [[claude-model-family]]. A system prompt, a Human turn and an Assistant turn are shown, and every token of the two turns is shaded by a single number.

That number comes from the [[reaction-concepts-protocol]]. Four empathetic words are fixed in advance as the reaction concepts: sorry, loss, grief and sympathy. At each token the [[jacobian-lens]] ranks the whole vocabulary, and the best rank any of the four words achieves is taken. That rank is then medianed over the [[workspace-layers]], roughly L38 to L92 on the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] scale.

Rank 1 shades a token deep orange. A rank at or past the axis floor leaves it white. The shading runs on a log scale, so most of the color range separates the top handful of ranks from each other.

The right half aggregates over the nine prompts in the suite. Four bars stand in two pairs: base model and Sonnet 4.5 on the user turn, then the same two on the Assistant turn. Each bar's height is the geometric mean, over the nine prompts, of the best rank reached anywhere in that turn.

The y axis is an inverted log scale, so rank 1 sits at the top and a taller bar means a better rank. One open circle per prompt is drawn on each bar, with a faint line joining that prompt's base and Sonnet 4.5 points, and hovering a circle opens the prompt text together with both models' [[j-lens-readout]] top-10 and the matched words highlighted.

On the Assistant turn the two models sit close together, with the empathetic words near the top of the readout in both. The paper says this is expected, since both models' responses express similar empathy — in the example shown, both say "I'm sorry for your loss".

On the user turn the two separate: Sonnet 4.5 ranks the words far higher than the base model does. The evidence is a suite of nine prompts and is descriptive rather than causal; nothing here tests whether the early [[j-space]] content changes what the model then writes.

terms.definition: The position of a token in the Jacobian lens's ranked list of the whole vocabulary at one residual-stream position and layer. Rank 1 means the lens scores that token above every other token there.

A short list of words fixed before the measurement, naming the reaction an Assistant would plausibly have to the prompt but which the prompt itself does not contain. The figure tracks only these words' ranks.
The four reaction concepts for the bereavement suite. At each token the best rank achieved by any one of the four is the value plotted and shaded.
The set of prompts behind this figure: a user mentions a recent loss in passing while asking about something practical, such as preserving a late relative's letters.
The pretrained model, trained only on next-token prediction, with no post-training. It is the gray series and the upper transcript, and the lens is applied to it identically.

The production assistant model corresponding to that base model, after post-training. It is the blue series and the lower transcript; the widget prints the label "Sonnet 4.5" where the underlying data says "post-trained".
The turn markers inside each transcript. The Human turn is the user's message; the Assistant turn is the model's own response, shown truncated.
The left pair of bars. Its value is the best reaction-concept rank reached at any token of the user's message, before the model has begun to answer.
The right pair of bars. Its value is the best reaction-concept rank reached at any token of the model's own response.
The y-axis label. The arrow points up because the axis is inverted: better (numerically smaller) ranks are higher on the chart.

The rank axis is logarithmic and runs from the floor at the bottom to rank 1 at the top, so bars grow upward as ranks improve and the gap between rank 1 and rank 5 gets as much room as the gap between 20 and 100.
Each bar's height. Ranks are multiplicative rather than additive quantities, so the nine per-prompt ranks are combined by geometric mean instead of an arithmetic average.
One small open circle per prompt, drawn on each bar at that prompt's own best rank, so the spread behind the geometric mean is visible.
A faint line joining one prompt's base-model circle to its Sonnet 4.5 circle within the same turn, showing the per-prompt change rather than only the group means.

The strip reading "Token shading = J-lens rank of empathetic words", with a white-to-orange color bar running from rank 1 to the floor. It maps transcript token background to the same rank quantity the bars use.

The bottom of the axis and of the color ramp. Any rank at or beyond it is clamped there, shown as white shading and reported in the tooltip with a "≥" sign, since the exact value no longer carries information.

The aggregation applied before ranking is compared across tokens: the reaction concepts' rank is taken at each layer in the workspace band and the median across those layers is used, so a spike at one isolated layer does not count.
The ten highest-ranked vocabulary tokens at the hovered prompt's best position, printed for both models, with any of the four reaction concepts highlighted.
The instruction text shown above the Human turn in each transcript. It is identical across the two models, so the transcripts differ only by which model reads them.
The mark closing a transcript whose Assistant response has been cut short for display. It signals truncation, not the end of the model's output.

The set of activations expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors — the region the paper argues acts as the model's workspace, and the thing the reaction concepts are said to enter early.

numbers.meaning: The number of bereavement prompts in the suite. Each contributes one circle per bar, and the bars are geometric means over these nine. It is a small suite, and the paper reports it as one of three such suites rather than as a benchmark.
The number of reaction concepts fixed for this suite — sorry, loss, grief, sympathy. Fixing them in advance is what makes the rank comparable across prompts and across the two models.
The models compared under an identical lens: the pretrained base model and its post-trained counterpart, Sonnet 4.5. The contrast between them is the figure's whole point.
Two spans are summarized — the user turn and the Assistant turn — and each is split by model, giving four bars. The Assistant-turn pair is drawn in a lighter tint of the same two colors.

The layer band over which each token's reaction-concept rank is medianed, on the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth scale. Section 4.1 identifies this range as the workspace layers: past the early layers where the J-space is empty, and before the final layers where readouts collapse onto the imminent output.

The best possible rank, at the top of the y axis and the dark end of the color ramp. A token shaded at rank 1 means one of the four empathetic words was the single highest-scoring token in the lens readout there.
The y-axis tick values. They are spaced logarithmically, so the visible distance between rank 1 and rank 2 is comparable to that between 50 and 100; the axis floor lies at or below the last tick.
The length of the ranked token list shown in the hover tooltip for each model. It is a display cutoff, not the measurement — the plotted rank is not capped at 10.
